- When sentiment is consistently negative or neutral (e.g., 0.00 or low values), model tends to overestimate prices; reduce forecast peaks and adjust downward bias.
- After a sharp price spike (e.g., >+5% from recent mean), model often overshoots and fails to correct — cap forecast peaks and add lagged mean reversion.
- If sentiment turns positive after a dip, model frequently underreacts — increase forecast slope slightly to match sentiment momentum.
- In low-sentiment periods (e.g., 0.00 for 10+ days), model overestimates mean reversion; reduce forecast volatility and align with recent 3-5 day average.
- For 30-day forecasts, model often overweights early days’ sentiment; weight later days’ sentiment more heavily (e.g., 70% last 7 days, 30% prior 20) to reduce lag bias.
- If true outcome shows strong mean reversion after a spike, model tends to overcorrect — adjust forecast to allow 1-2 day lag before reversal.
- When sentiment is high and price is rising, model often underestimates continuation — increase forecast slope slightly to match sentiment momentum.
- Avoid overfitting to recent highs — if last 3 days are above 90, cap forecast at 92–93 unless sentiment strongly supports higher price.
